Here is a detailed comparison between the **first satellite ever launched** and one of the **latest satellites launched in 2026**:

---

# 🛰️ First Satellite vs. Latest Satellite (2026)

---

## 🚀 FIRST SATELLITE: Sputnik 1 (1957)

Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite, launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on **4 October 1957**.

- **Size & Shape:** It was a polished metal sphere **58 cm (23 in) in diameter** with four external radio antennas to broadcast radio pulses.
- **Weight:** Sputnik 1 was an **83.6 kg (184-pound)** capsule.
- **Instruments/Payload:** It was a metal sphere with four long antennas protruding from it, and it contained **a thermometer, a fan, a radio transmitter, batteries, and little else.**
- **Orbit:** Sputnik 1's orbit was elliptical — approximately **230 km** from Earth at its closest point (perigee) and **940 km** away at its furthest point (apogee). It took just under an hour and a half to circle the entire planet.
- **Speed:** It orbited Earth at **29,000 km/h (18,000 miles per hour)**.
- **Mission Duration:** It sent a radio signal back to Earth for **three weeks** before its batteries became depleted. Aerodynamic drag caused it to fall back into the atmosphere on **4 January 1958**.
- **Purpose:** The only cargo onboard Sputnik was a **low-power radio transmitter**, which broadcast a beeping noise at regular intervals.
- **Impact:** The Sputnik launch marked the **start of the space age** and the US-USSR space race, and led to the creation of NASA.

---

## 🛰️ LATEST MAJOR SATELLITE: ViaSat-3 F3 (2026)

ViaSat-3 Flight 3 (VS-3 F3) successfully launched from **Kennedy Space Center in Florida** aboard a **SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket** on **April 29, 2026**.

- **Orbit:** The Falcon Heavy delivered the satellite to a favorable transfer orbit where the satellite's **electric propulsion** takes over to place it in **geostationary orbit (GEO)**, where it will spend several months traveling before arriving at its reserved orbital slot.
- **Purpose/Payload:** ViaSat-3 F3 is the final satellite in the ViaSat-3 constellation and is designed to expand Viasat's global network with **more than 1 Tbps of throughput** over the **Asia-Pacific region**.
- **Technology:** The ViaSat-3 satellites are designed with **state-of-the-art technology** to maximize efficient, flexible bandwidth deployment and provide enhanced performance for commercial mobility, fixed services, and defense customers.
- **Capabilities:** Each of the new VS-3 satellites is expected to support **more bandwidth capacity than Viasat's entire existing fleet** and support key growth initiatives in aviation, maritime, and government satellite communications.
- **Standards:** Viasat believes the VS-3 satellites are the most advanced commercial satellites in the world in terms of **adaptive beamforming** for cost efficiencies and user performance, and that they set new commercial standards for **solar power generation and thermal dissipation**.
- **Service Entry:** Following launch, the satellite will spend several months traveling to geostationary orbit, then undergo rigorous in-orbit testing, with service entry **expected by late summer 2026**.

---

## 📊 Side-by-Side Comparison

| Feature | 🛸 Sputnik 1 (1957) | 🛰️ ViaSat-3 F3 (2026) |
|---|---|---|
| **Launch Date** | October 4, 1957 | April 29, 2026 |
| **Launched By** | Soviet Union | Viasat / SpaceX |
| **Launch Vehicle** | Modified R-7 rocket | SpaceX Falcon Heavy |
| **Weight** | 83.6 kg (184 lbs) | Several thousand kg (GEO-class) |
| **Size** | 58 cm sphere (beach ball) | Large bus-sized satellite |
| **Orbit** | Low Earth Orbit (230–940 km) | Geostationary Orbit (~35,786 km) |
| **Speed** | ~29,000 km/h | ~11,000 km/h (GEO) |
| **Payload** | Radio transmitter + thermometer | 1+ Terabit/sec broadband payload |
| **Mission Life** | ~92 days | 15–20+ years |
| **Coverage** | Limited (signal detection) | Entire Asia-Pacific region |
| **Purpose** | Prove satellite orbit was possible | Global broadband communications |

---

## 🔑 Key Takeaway

The difference between these two satellites illustrates an extraordinary ~69-year leap in technology. Sputnik 1 was only 58 cm in diameter and weighed 83 kg, making it very small and light compared to today's satellites. Modern geostationary communications satellites can weigh as much as **7,000 kg — over eighty times as much** as Sputnik 1. What was once a beeping metal ball has evolved into a sophisticated, solar-powered platform delivering terabits of data across entire continents!
